statements.text: How can we start beginning to aggregate, to concentrate around agreed common definitions of what fairness—and fairness is one of the most closely held moral values among most Americans? Why is it so important that policymakers start to align fairness policies?
statements.context: Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness during a Senate hearing on securing U.S. leadership in emerging compute technologies.

statements.text: The trustworthy AI systems are more fair, more transparent, more explainable, more robust, I think in many cases.
statements.context: Senate hearing on emerging compute technologies where the senator asks a final question before departing for a floor vote.

statements.text: One, artificial intelligence, AI, has the power to automate complex processes and improve our efficiency in every sector of our economy.
statements.context: Senate hearing on emerging compute technologies where Senator Hickenlooper delivered opening remarks on AI, quantum information science, and blockchain.

statements.text: Absolutely. Ms. Espinel, increasing the transparency of AI systems is one of the key vehicles by which we gain confidence and trust among the users. Without appropriate guardrails around the risks from AI, I think developers will struggle to compete in the U.S., and certainly internationally as well. So it is in our best interest to demonstrate leadership, and safe and responsible deployment. What transparency steps do you prioritize; do you think are most crucial in terms of gaining the trust of consumers?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'The Need for Transparency in Artificial Intelligence,' during a Q&A exchange between Senator Hickenlooper and a witness.

statements.text: How can we create an oversight and enforcement framework to make sure that we can hold bad actors accountable? You know, people that use the AI systems maliciously?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'The Need for Transparency in Artificial Intelligence,' during a Q&A exchange with industry witnesses.

statements.text: Dr. Krishnan, you have done a lot of research with consumers and social behavior within digital environments, so on that same subject, what information should be disclosed to consumers to establish trust in online services around AI?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'The Need for Transparency in Artificial Intelligence', where Senator Hickenlooper questions an expert witness.

statements.text: But we must also confront the fact that AI can be misused by bad actors, AI can be used to make scams, fraud, and cyber attacks more harmful, and more effective. [...] Congress will play a role by setting reasonable rules of the road to inform and protect consumers.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Senator Hickenlooper at a Senate Commerce Subcommittee hearing on AI transparency.

statements.text: Unfortunately, the Biden Administration and some of my colleagues in Congress have embraced doomsday AI scenarios as justification for expanded Federal regulation. Some of these proposals are extremely onerous: Licensing regimes, creating a new regulatory agency to police computer code, and mandatory, NEPA-style impact assessments before AI can be used.
statements.context: Prepared statement submitted for the record of a Senate subcommittee hearing on AI transparency.

statements.text: I recently was informed about a situation in my state that I found quite alarming. A family in Pierce County, Washington, received a phone call. A scammer used AI to spoof the voice of their daughter [...] And a recent deepfake image claimed a bombing occurred at the Pentagon, and that fake image sparked a dip in the stock market. DARPA is leading the way on important developments to approach detecting AI-generated media. And I plan to introduce legislation in this area. [...] I know that we need to grow education, in general, in our workforce. And the information age has already put great transformations in place. The jobs of tomorrow are here today, but the skill levels for people to do them are not.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee hearing on AI transparency, where the chair shares constituent cases of AI-enabled fraud and outlines her planned legislative response.

statements.text: AI systems learn about the world by processing written, visual, and audio files, works created by people, by humans. [...] what rights already exist for consumers to decide how AI systems access their creations, and what additional rights do they have?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "The Need for Transparency in Artificial Intelligence," where Senator Hickenlooper questions an expert witness panel.

statements.text: NIST is the standard-setting body. They are kind of the lead agency now in the Administration's work on AI. They have already put out their Risk Management Framework, which is voluntary risk guides for developers developing AI. [...] And that is the entity that will be forming the new standards.
statements.context: Senate hearing on CHIPS and Science Act implementation where Senator Hickenlooper questions Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo about federal AI standards strategy.

statements.text: It will be important to make sure that workers can access the trainings that meet a variety of skills and skill requirements. As this all happened so fast—these transitions are going so quickly, the potential that I think you lay out there that, that AI can be a tool to take intellectual property and violate the cost and the creation of that capital. What are some of—what do you imagine as some of the solutions that would protect companies to—in that situation?
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI and the future of work where Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness about workforce transitions and IP protection.

statements.text: Ms.Morley Ryan and I think what we have seen with a lot of the questions and responses is that the balance between risk and opportunity that AI poses, and I think, I feel that we have an alliance of people that are more excited by the opportunity.
statements.context: Senator Hickenlooper chairs a Senate hearing on AI and the future of work, questioning a witness about workforce training and small business adoption of AI.

statements.text: Just yesterday, President Biden signed an Executive Order focused on AI governance, a critical step in our Nation's overall approach to how we integrate AI into a larger and larger parts of our life.
statements.context: Opening statement by Senator Hickenlooper at a Senate Subcommittee hearing on AI and the future of work.

statements.text: There are a number of ways that AI obviously can enhance workplace processes [...] This could go too far, and we run the risk of relying too much on AI, I think at—potentially at the expense of human decision-making. Imagine decision-making being a muscle that atrophies.
statements.context: Senator Hickenlooper poses a question to an industry panel during a hearing on AI and the future of work.

statements.text: Dr. Inglesby, you spoke about the potential for AI models to assist malicious actors in creating highly transmissible pathogens. This is obviously all the more possible given that we do not currently require screening for all gene synthesis providers. Senator Budd and I have a bill called the Gene Synthesis Safety and Security Act, which would help us conduct critical oversight of the industry and protect against misuse of these types of products.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in health care, during a Q&A round with expert witness Dr. Inglesby.

statements.text: certainly, AI could be a great equalizer in terms of helping us to amass and analyze all and connect all those data points. [...] How can we seize on this moment with our AI to catapult our ability to utilize real world data, but also building the guardrails that you have all been saying are necessary to ensure the security of the data.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in health care, where Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness on balancing AI-driven data utilization with data security guardrails.

statements.text: does increased reliance on AI and other technologies introduce new security threats that we should address on the front end?
statements.context: Senate hearing on cyber threats to critical water and energy infrastructure, where Senator Hickenlooper asks expert witnesses about AI's benefits and risks for grid modernization.

statements.text: training AI systems cannot be—it really cannot be at the expense of people's privacy and reducing the amount of personal sets of data, as you have all discussed, the notion of minimization does really reduce the likelihood that data privacy and data security harm could happen.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee hearing on consumer privacy and AI, with Senator Hickenlooper questioning a witness.

statements.text: S. 4769. A bill to require the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop voluntary guidelines and specifications for internal and external assurances of artificial intelligence systems, and for other purposes; to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
statements.context: Introduction of bills in the Senate on July 24, 2024, where newly filed bills are read by title and referred to committee.

statements.text: While we work toward that goal, however, the National Electric Reliability Cooperation, as well as the Bravo Group, projected, as we have just been discussing, significant increases in demand on the grid in part from data centers that are training and running these AI systems. So Dr. Kaushik, how much do we know, and what more information do we need about what our benefit is here? In other words, how much more electricity will AI and these emerging technologies require, and how can we begin to estimate the benefits and the savings in energy that they will provide us?
statements.context: Senate committee hearing on the Department of Energy's role in advanced computing research, application, and security.

statements.text: the National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST) has established the U.S. AI Safety Institute to work with government agencies and the private sector to develop metrics and benchmarks and tests that ensure AI systems are both safe and reliable. [...] Ms. Fu, could you describe how DOE collaborates with NIST and NSF and other agencies, but that collaboration to advance AI safety research which, I think, you know, we are getting the cart before the horse here a little bit.
statements.context: Senate hearing examining the Department of Energy's role in advanced computing research and AI safety.

statements.text: as some employers have been experimenting with AI applications, we have seen that creating opportunities for workers to provide feedback is important. [...] What steps are you taking, or should others be taking, to collect feedback from workers about their experiences as they interact with these AI applications? And how would that feedback impact your efforts going forward?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "Reading the Room: Preparing Workers for AI," where Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness about worker feedback on AI in the workplace.

statements.text: AI literacy should also include an emphasis on methods to help workers identify AI generated content versus human generated content.
statements.context: Opening statement by Senator Hickenlooper, Chair of the Subcommittee on Employment and Workplace Safety, at a hearing on preparing workers for AI.

statements.text: But I think that this notion of where do we get our standards, how do we codify, what is the appropriate way to do this, it ties back into that—a little bit of that disadvantage that we have compared to totalitarian countries where they could just decide that everything is going to be somehow watermarked or that transparency on what is and what is not AI.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'Reading the Room: Preparing Workers for AI,' where Senator Hickenlooper questions witnesses about AI standards and transparency.

statements.text: aiEDU is launching AI literacy initiatives across the country including a recently launched partnership in Colorado. How do you work with local leaders and employers to help customize the training resources and ensure that they are responsive to local or regional training needs?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "Reading the Room: Preparing Workers for AI," during the Q&A portion.

statements.text: But I think we recognize and should all own up to the fact that scammers are already using this new technology to prey on innocent consumers.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Senator Hickenlooper as Chair of the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection, Product Safety, and Data Security, at a hearing on AI-enabled fraud and scams.

statements.text: We have seen AI technology evolve so rapidly the last few years I think we have to anticipate that that trend is going to continue and probably accelerate. [...] As AI continues to evolve how would you see data privacy protections helping to mitigate fraud against consumers?
statements.context: Senate hearing on protecting consumers from AI-enabled fraud and scams, chaired by Senator Hickenlooper.

statements.text: Ms. Mani, you have discussed the need for increased AI literacy in our schools, really, at all ages, whether elementary school or all the way through high school. [...] when you look at benefits and risks how do you—what do you present to our students?
statements.context: Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness during a Senate Commerce Committee hearing on protecting consumers from AI-enabled fraud and scams.

statements.text: Dr. Farid, you discussed different tools and techniques available for detecting AI-generated media including, you know, humans manually labeling content and automated detection tools. How effective are the different kinds of tools and techniques to detect deepfakes and, you know, all these things from voices to video how well are they working?
statements.context: Senate hearing on protecting consumers from AI-enabled fraud and scams, where Senator Hickenlooper questions an expert witness.

statements.text: In terms of recognizing the immense power of these very large companies and what we have seen with social platforms and in many cases the lack of any ability of Government to curtail some of the things we recognize are—I mean, some of the deepfake pornography, that is one example that comes up. How do you think we should be looking at AI on that same—within that same context of being able to get the market to have some balance?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for the OSTP Director nominee, where Hickenlooper questions the nominee about AI oversight.

statements.text: What are the internal processes that Microsoft follows to evaluate Copilot's accuracy and performance before it was released and what kind of independent review teams other than Microsoft's own product developers are involved in that? Who do you bring in to help with that?
statements.context: Senate hearing on U.S. AI capabilities where a senator questions a Microsoft executive about product evaluation practices.

statements.text: the bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act, an historic effort to try and maintain U.S. leadership in emerging technologies like semiconductors but others as well, as the technology arms race continues globally [...] the new chips that are going to power our electronics and the devices that are going to allow AI to become global. [...] what do you see as the next frontier of chip technology in terms of energy efficiency and how can—and that is not just based on the Chinese competitors but how can we work together to improve direct to chip cooling for high-performance computing?
statements.context: Senate hearing on strengthening U.S. computing and innovation capabilities, featuring testimony from AMD CEO Dr. Lisa Su.

statements.text: Mr. Secretary, accelerating the deployment of new nuclear energy is something that I think you agree is critical to the U.S. achieving global energy dominance and meeting our needs, our energy demands, our national security needs, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence and the emerging AI race that is surrounding that. [...] Can you discuss with us the Department's authority to authorize nuclear projects, including reactors and fuel cycle facilities, and just describe for us how the Department may use that authority to speed up the development and the deployment of new nuclear energy and whether Congress ought to consider any legislative changes beyond that to help expand that authority?
statements.context: Senate hearing on the DOE FY 2026 budget request, where the Chairman (Senator Hickenlooper) asks Secretary Wright about nuclear-energy permitting reform driven by AI-driven energy demand.

statements.text: I think we all agree with you that we have got to win the AI race. And it's not just our economic future, it's our national security that's at stake there.
statements.context: Senate hearing on challenges to meeting increased electricity demand, where Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness about transmission infrastructure and AI competitiveness.

statements.text: Would you agree that the probability of our losing ground in the race toward AI, the probability that we are going to lose ground increases if we don't address this issue within the grid?
statements.context: Senator Hickenlooper questioning a witness on electricity grid challenges during a Senate hearing on increased power demand.

statements.text: Great. Appreciate that. The Action Plan calls for Federal agencies to conduct independent evaluations of AI systems before they are procured and deployed. Independent evaluation will help enhance security and increase trust, prevents companies from grading their own homework, as we would say, after an AI model is developed.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled "AI've Got a Plan: America's AI Action Plan" where Senator Hickenlooper questions a witness about AI evaluation frameworks.

statements.text: It might include periodic impact assessments to evaluate potential risk on AI models, transparency disclosures to users describing AI models in terms of use and capabilities. Obviously need R&D for support for standards development to identify and detect AI-generated content, and transparency around that. Privacy protections for certain types of data being used to train AI models.
statements.context: Senate hearing at which the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director was questioned about elements of a potential federal AI statute.

statements.text: The Trump Administration won't take no for an answer on a moratorium on state AI laws without a Federal standard. [...] Instead of trying to preempt laws that protect against AI fraud or theft, we need to be protecting consumers.
statements.context: Written questions submitted by Senator Hickenlooper to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr following a December 17, 2025 FCC oversight hearing.

statements.text: The United States is remaining a global leader in innovation including AI. I think that is a goal that is broadly bipartisan. As a former Governor in Colorado, I recognize that states are, rightfully, the laboratories of democracy. The President's recent executive order on AI directs the FCC to consider withholding funds to states that have AI laws that could be in conflict with stated goals. Obviously, I think the FCC does have a role in how AI is involved in managing communication networks or blocking robocalls. I think it is questionable at best whether the FCC can regulate how AI models are used or developed. So let me start with Commissioner Gomez. Does the FCC have explicit jurisdiction under the Communications Act to preempt state AI laws? Why or why not?
statements.context: Senate oversight hearing on the FCC, Senator Hickenlooper questioning commissioners on FCC authority over AI regulation and state law preemption.

statements.text: Only one in ten teachers report receiving training or information on how—what to do if they suspect this is the case, how they should respond.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the impact of technology on youth, where Senator Hickenlooper questions an expert witness about student AI use and educator preparedness.
